newsitem.title: INDIA: India relaxes import controls, sees rupee stable.
newsitem.headline: India relaxes import controls, sees rupee stable.

text.p: India's commerce minister, shrugging off a political setback to the coalition government, unveiled on Monday a new trade policy that lifted import controls on hundreds of items.

Bolla Buli Ramaiah also said the rupee, riding on the strength of a surge in foreign exchange reserves, would remain stable despite an announcement on Sunday by the Congress party that it would withdraw its make-or-break support to the minority United Front government.

The five-year export-import policy, which would take effect on April 1, shifted 542 items out of a list of restricted imports and allowed them to be imported freely or under easily transferable licences. Details were expected later on Monday.
The policy also cut red tape and simplified procedures.

But consumer electronics and cotton textiles remained on the restricted import list, symbolising lingering socialist controls in an economy that has undergone a far-reaching free-market reform programme since 1991.

"As we move towards further liberalisation and globalisation, we need to focus on areas where we have strength and advantage to meet global competition as also such areas which have trade potential," Ramaiah said in a statement.
"This is the rationale for expanding the freely importable list and further pruning the negative list," he said.
Industry welcomed the new policy.
Shekhar Datta, president of the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII), complimented the minister "for keeping his promise to present a dynamic exim policy...", the CII said in a statement.

Ramaiah said he expected the rupee to remain stable because of strong foreign exchange reserves. "Today we have more than $22 billion of reserves," Ramaiah told Reuters. "Definitely it (rupee) will stabilise. Absolutely no problem."

The rupee, held down by aggressive purchases of the dollar by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) earlier this month, on Monday opened 10 paise lower at 35.99 per dollar, and was trading at 35.875 rupees at 1030 GMT.
Foreign exchange reserves including gold stood at $25.1 billion on March 21, compared with $21.4 billion a year ago.

The surge is linked to a rise in capital inflows linked to industry-friendly tax cuts proposed in the budget for 1997/98 (April-March), parliamentary approval for which is now threatened by the current political uncertainties.

The Congress party on Monday said Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda should "gracefully resign" and his coalition should support a new Congress-led government. It accused Deve Gowda of failing to check the growth of communalism among other reasons.
Deve Gowda said he was not planning to resign and would face parliament.

Officials said India's trade deficit in 1996/97, ending on Monday, was expected to be around $5.0 billion on account of a slowdown in exports, which were expected to be around $33-34 billion compared with $31.83 billion in 1995/96, when exports rose 21.38 percent from $26.22 billion in 1994/95.
"The reduction is on account of a few commodities mainly in the plantation sector like tea, coffee and rice," said Commerce Secretary P.P. Prabhu, the top-ranking ministry bureaucrat.
"In addition, in certain crucial sectors we have a setback like gems and jewellery," he added.

The policy statement said the government would increase the number of agencies that can sell gold to jewellery exporters and allow export-oriented units in the sector to sell 10 percent of their output in the domestic market.
The new policy also permitted dedicated exporters of agricultural and electronic hardware goods to sell 50 percent of the value of their annual output in the domestic market.
The policy cut import duty on capital goods linked to exports to 10 percent from 15 percent.
Prabhu said India's efforts to lift quantitative restrictions on imports were not linked to its commitments to the World Trade Organisation (WTO).
"Shifting of the 542 items is not a part of the phase-out plan," Prabhu said. "The phase-out plan is still under discussion in the government," he said.
"The aim is to facilitate exporters to get quality raw materials at internationally competitive rates in a hassle-free environment without extra cost," Prabhu said.
